
```{r}
library(adempR)
```

Every method is applied to the same simulated data sets. This pairing is
the main source of precision when methods are compared: two methods that
both have a coverage MCSE of 0.007 can have a coverage difference with an
MCSE of 0.002, because their errors are correlated. Comparing two
separately estimated values with their separate MCSEs throws that
information away.

## Mean versus median under heavy tails

```{r}
study <- sim_study("center",
  scenarios = sim_scenarios(n = c(20L, 80L), df = c(3, 30)),
  generate = function(scenario, context) rt(scenario$n, scenario$df),
  estimands = list(sim_estimand("center", sim_truth_exact(function(scenario) 0))),
  methods = list(
    mean = function(data) {
      tt <- t.test(data)
      sim_estimate("center", mean(data), se = sd(data) / sqrt(length(data)),
                   lower = tt$conf.int[1], upper = tt$conf.int[2], level = 0.95)
    },
    median = function(data) {
      w <- suppressWarnings(wilcox.test(data, conf.int = TRUE))
      sim_estimate("center", median(data), lower = w$conf.int[1],
                   upper = w$conf.int[2], level = 0.95)
    }),
  measures = c("bias", "empse", "rmse", "coverage", "width"))
run <- sim_run(study, replications = 300, seed = 8, path = file.path(tempdir(), "center"))
```

## Paired differences

For a measure that is a mean of per replication contributions (bias, MAE,
MSE, coverage, width, rejection, usable), the difference between methods
is the mean of the per replication differences, and its MCSE is their
standard deviation over $\sqrt n$.

```{r}
cmp <- sim_compare(run, c("mean", "median"),
                   measures = c("mse", "coverage", "width", "relative_precision"),
                   bootstrap = 300)
cmp[c("scenario_id", "measure", "value", "mcse", "lower", "upper", "correlation", "n_common")]
```

Differences are the second method minus the first (the reference). The
`correlation` column shows how strongly the methods' contributions are
paired.

## Relative precision

Relative precision compares empirical variances:
$100\,(\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta_A) / \operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta_B) - 1)$,
where $A$ is the reference method and $B$ the compared method. Positive
values mean the compared method is more precise than the reference. The
interval and the reported MCSE come from a paired bootstrap over
replications, which resamples both methods together. The note also gives
the analytic MCSE of Morris, White and Crowther (2019),
$200\,\frac{\operatorname{Var}_A}{\operatorname{Var}_B}\sqrt{\frac{1-\rho^2}{n-1}}$
with $\rho$ the correlation between the estimates, which assumes bivariate
normal estimates and can be too small for heavy tailed data such as these.
`empse_ratio` and `rmse_ratio` use the same bootstrap; when more than 1
percent of resamples are undefined (a zero denominator) the interval is
withheld with status `unstable`.

With $t_3$ data the median is more precise than the mean; with $t_{30}$
data the mean wins.

## Equivalence margins

A difference can be statistically clear and scientifically irrelevant.
Give a margin to flag comparisons whose whole interval lies inside it.
For differences the margin is around 0; for the ratios `empse_ratio` and
`rmse_ratio` it is relative, around 1. When every paired difference is
equal (for coverage: no data set where one method covers and the other
does not), the MCSE is 0 and says nothing about agreement; such rows get
status `boundary` and no equivalence flag.

```{r}
eq <- sim_compare(run, c("mean", "median"), measures = "coverage", margin = 0.02)
eq[c("scenario_id", "value", "lower", "upper", "within_margin")]
```

## The comparison population

When methods fail on different data sets, a conditional measure such as
coverage is computed on different subsets for each method. `sim_compare()`
always uses the replications where both methods are eligible, and reports
`n_common`. Read conditional comparisons together with the `usable`
comparison, which uses all generated data sets. See
`vignette("failures-and-denominators")`.

## No single winner

Methods trade bias against variance, coverage against width, and accuracy
against failures and run time. `sim_pareto()` marks, in each scenario, the
methods that are not dominated on the chosen criteria. It does not rank or
aggregate across scenarios, because there is rarely a defensible way to
weight them.

```{r}
pv <- sim_pareto(sim_summarise(run, c("rmse", "width", "usable")),
                 c(rmse = "min", width = "min", usable = "max"))
pv
```
